questions.question: In an undirected network, possibly with several parallel edges between the same two vertices, how is the degree of a vertex $v$ defined?
options: The number of edges at $v$, each parallel edge counted.
The number of different vertices joined to $v$ by an edge.
The total length of the edges incident to $v$.
Twice the number of edges incident to $v$, one per end.

questions.question: An undirected network has edge set $E$, possibly with parallel edges, and $\deg v$ denotes the degree of vertex $v$. What is the sum of $\deg v$ over all vertices $v$, and why?
options: $|E|$, since each edge is counted at one vertex.
The number of vertices, since each vertex has one degree.
$2$ times the number of vertices, one per edge end.
$2|E|$, since each edge has two ends, at two vertices.

questions.question: In an undirected network, vertex $v$ lies on no edge at all. What is the degree of $v$, and is it even or odd?
options: Degree 0, which counts as an even degree.
Degree 0, which is neither even nor odd.
Degree 1, as $v$ still counts itself.
Undefined, since $v$ has no neighbours.

questions.question: In an undirected network, vertex $A$ is joined to $B$ by two parallel edges and to $C$ by one edge, and to nothing else. How do the degree of $A$ and the number of its neighbours compare?
options: Both are 2, since $A$ is joined to $B$ and $C$.
$\deg A=3$, which is one more than its 2 neighbours.
Both are 3, since degree and neighbours always agree.
$A$ has 3 neighbours but only 2 incident edges.

questions.question: In a weighted undirected network, vertex $v$ has exactly three incident edges, of lengths 2, 4 and 6. Is the degree of $v$ even or odd?
options: Odd, since exactly three edges meet at $v$.
Even, since the total incident length 12 is even.
Even, since each incident length is even.
Odd, since the largest incident length is 6.

questions.question: An undirected network has edges $A\text{-}B$, $A\text{-}C$, $A\text{-}D$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$ and $D\text{-}E$. Which vertices have odd degree?
options: $A$, $C$ and $D$ only
$A$, $C$, $D$ and $E$
$E$ only
$B$ and $E$

questions.question: An undirected network has five vertices with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2 and 4. How many edges does it have?
A planner lists proposed vertex degrees for an undirected network with five vertices, where parallel edges are allowed. Which list cannot be the degrees of any such network?
An undirected network has 10 edges. Vertex $v$ has degree 4. Vertex $v$ is removed together with all edges at $v$. What is the sum of the degrees of the remaining vertices?
An undirected network gets one new edge between two different vertices $u$ and $v$. By how much can the number of odd-degree vertices change?
options: By $-2$, $0$ or $+2$, depending on the old parities.
Always by $+2$, since two degrees increase.
By $+1$ or $-1$, since one vertex changes parity.
Never, since adding one edge keeps the degree sum even.

questions.question: In an undirected network, every edge of a path from $s$ to $t$ (with $s\ne t$) is duplicated by adding a parallel copy. How do the parities of the degrees change?
options: Every vertex on the path changes parity.
No vertex changes parity, as edges are added in pairs.
$s$ and $t$ change parity; inner path vertices keep it.
Only the inner vertices change parity.

questions.question: An undirected network has $n$ vertices and no parallel edges, so at most one edge joins any two vertices. What is the largest possible degree of a vertex?
options: $n$, one edge to every vertex of the network.
No limit, since a vertex may have many edges.
$n-1$, one edge to each of the other vertices.
$n-2$, as one other vertex must stay unjoined.

questions.question: An undirected network has edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}A$ and $A\text{-}C$. A parallel copy is added to each edge of the path $A\text{-}B\text{-}C$. Which vertices have odd degree afterwards?
options: Only vertex $B$
Vertices $A$ and $C$
Vertices $B$ and $D$
No vertex at all

questions.question: An undirected network has edges $A\text{-}B$, $B\text{-}C$, $C\text{-}D$, $D\text{-}E$, $E\text{-}A$, $B\text{-}E$ and $C\text{-}E$. Which single extra edge (parallel edges allowed) makes every vertex degree even?
options: A new edge $B\text{-}D$
A new edge $A\text{-}D$
No single edge; two are needed
A second edge $B\text{-}C$

questions.question: In an undirected network the degrees satisfy $\sum_v\deg v=2|E|$. Why must the number of vertices of odd degree be even?
options: Only in connected networks, since odd vertices pair up along paths.
Because each odd vertex has an odd vertex as neighbour.
Only when no parallel edges occur.
Even degrees add to an even number, so the odd ones must too.

questions.question: Four vertices $A,B,C,D$ should get degrees 3, 3, 0 and 0. The degree sum 6 is even. Can such an undirected network be built, and does it matter whether parallel edges are allowed?
options: Yes in both cases, since an even degree sum is sufficient.
Only with parallel edges: three edges joining $A$ and $B$.
No in both cases, since $A$ and $B$ have odd degree.
Only without parallel edges, as they would double degrees.

questions.question: An undirected network on four vertices has no parallel edges. Which list of four vertex degrees cannot occur, although its sum is even?
